::: {.takeaway}
**Takeaway.** A panel of reference annotators is reliable for a model–human comparison if it reaches the same conclusion as the latent target. We develop a test that identifies reliable panels without observing the latent target and controls the probability of a false certification, and we apply it to real chest X-ray annotations from VinDr-CXR.
:::

In this part, we consider the aggregate-score setting of [I.1](#aggregate-score): each radiologist's $27$ binary labels on an image are averaged into one score, modeled as a continuous variable in $[0,1],$ on which the models are trained and the model–human comparisons are made. [Part III](#part-3) considers the binary labels of [I.2](#binary-labels).

### Which reference can be reliable?

[Part I](#part-1) shows that the training annotator is not a neutral reference for model–human comparison. A natural replacement is an independent annotator C, but C has a bias $b_C$ of its own, which also enters the comparison. Then when can an independent annotator serve as a neutral reference? Alternatively, one can construct the reference from the labels of several annotators [@warfield2004simultaneous; @irvin2019chexpert], but how many annotators are enough? Both questions ask when a (set of) reference annotator(s) is reliable. In this part, we develop a statistical test of whether an evaluation reference is reliable for a given model–human comparison, that is, whether it leads to the same conclusion as the latent target.

### Challenges from sparse labels

A reference built from several annotators requires their scores on the same evaluation images. In practice, however, this is often expensive or unavailable. In VinDr-CXR, for example, each training image is labeled by only three of the $17$ radiologists, so a set of reference annotators other than A and B rarely labels the same images. To resolve this issue, we train a predictor $\widehat\mu_r$ on the labels of each reference annotator $r.$ Like $\widehat\mu_A$ in [I.1](#aggregate-score), it targets $r$'s conditional mean $\mu_r,$ so its predictions on the evaluation images can serve as a surrogate for $r$'s labels. We call $\widehat\mu_r$ the *surrogate predictor* of annotator $r.$

Let $\mathcal R$ be the set of reference annotators, which excludes A and B, and let $K$ be its size, the number of annotators asked about above. We let *evaluation reference* be the average of the surrogate predictors:

$$
\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(x)
=\frac1K\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}\widehat\mu_r(x).
$$

As for $\widehat\mu_A$ in [I.1](#aggregate-score), write $\widehat\mu_r=\mu_r+\widehat e_r$ with learning error $\widehat e_r.$ We make two assumptions on this error, for every $r\in\mathcal R:$

- **Centered error:** $\mathbb E_X[\widehat e_r(X)]=0.$ Averaged over items, the surrogate predictor neither overestimates nor underestimates annotator $r$'s mean score.
- **Independence:** $\widehat e_r(X)\perp\big(\widehat\mu_A(X)-Y_B(X)\big),$ as random variables of the item $X$ and B's annotation noise, with all trained predictors held fixed. The error of a surrogate predictor on an item is unrelated to the difference between the model and B on that item.

Together, they give the orthogonality condition, for every $r\in\mathcal R,$

$$
\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[\widehat e_r(X)\,(\widehat\mu_A(X)-Y_B(X))\big]=0.
$$ {#eq-reference-orthogonality}

Both assumptions require the surrogate predictors to be trained on data disjoint from the evaluation images.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Deriving the orthogonality condition"}

With all trained predictors held fixed, the independence assumption lets the expectation of the product factor into a product of expectations. Since $\widehat e_r(X)$ does not depend on the annotation noise, its expectation reduces to an average over items, which vanishes by the centered-error assumption:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[\widehat e_r(X)\,(\widehat\mu_A(X)-Y_B(X))\big]
&=\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[\widehat e_r(X)\big]\;\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[\widehat\mu_A(X)-Y_B(X)\big]\\
&=\mathbb E_X\big[\widehat e_r(X)\big]\;\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[\widehat\mu_A(X)-Y_B(X)\big]=0.
\end{aligned}
$$

:::

### Reliability for a specific comparison

The model–human comparison asks whether the model or annotator B is closer to the latent target $\mu^*.$ If $\mu^*$ were observed, the comparison would be decided by the sign of the latent gap

$$
\Delta^*
=\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}[(\widehat\mu_A(X)-\mu^*(X))^2-(Y_B(X)-\mu^*(X))^2].
$$ {#eq-latent-gap}

With the evaluation reference in place of $\mu^*,$ it is decided by the sign of

$$
\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}
=\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}[(\widehat\mu_A(X)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X))^2
-(Y_B(X)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X))^2].
$$

We call the evaluation reference *reliable* for this comparison if the two gaps have the same nonzero sign, so that both name the same better performer.

How far can the two gaps differ? Replacing $\mu^*$ with the evaluation reference changes the gap by

$$
\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}-\Delta^*
=-2g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}},
\qquad
g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}
=\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}[(\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X)-\mu^*(X))(\widehat\mu_A(X)-Y_B(X))].
$$ {#eq-reference-distortion}

The two gaps must have the same sign whenever $\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ exceeds this change in magnitude:

$$
|\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|>|\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}-\Delta^*|=2|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|.
$$ {#eq-population-certificate}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Deriving the change in the gap"}

Subtracting @eq-latent-gap from the definition of $\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ and applying $u^2-v^2=(u-v)(u+v)$ to the model terms and to B's terms separately,

$$
\begin{aligned}
\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}-\Delta^*
&=\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[(\widehat\mu_A(X)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X))^2-(\widehat\mu_A(X)-\mu^*(X))^2\big]
-\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[(Y_B(X)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X))^2-(Y_B(X)-\mu^*(X))^2\big]\\
&=\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[(\mu^*(X)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X))\big(2\widehat\mu_A(X)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X)-\mu^*(X)\big)\big]
-\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[(\mu^*(X)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X))\big(2Y_B(X)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X)-\mu^*(X)\big)\big]\\
&=-2\,\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}\big[(\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X)-\mu^*(X))(\widehat\mu_A(X)-Y_B(X))\big].
\end{aligned}
$$

Since $\Delta^*=\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}+2g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}},$ the two gaps share a nonzero sign if and only if $\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}(\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}+2g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}})>0,$ which holds whenever $|\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|>2|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|.$

:::

The condition in @eq-population-certificate cannot be checked directly: the gap $\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ can be estimated from the evaluation images, but $g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ involves the unobserved latent target. We therefore develop a test that bounds $g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ using how the reference annotators differ from one another, and certifies the reference when the estimated gap clearly exceeds this bound.

### Testing reliability from data

The test uses two sets of images labeled by B: a set $D_1$ of $n_1$ images, on which the gap is estimated, and a calibration set $D_2$ of $n_2$ images, on which the bound on $|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|$ is calibrated. The two sets may coincide.

#### The Gaussian assumption

We treat the $K$ reference annotators as random draws from the annotator population, so the quantities

$$
g_{\widehat r}
=\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}[(\widehat\mu_r(X)-\mu^*(X))(\widehat\mu_A(X)-Y_B(X))],
\qquad r\in\mathcal R,
$$

are random, and so is their average $g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}:=K^{-1}\sum_{r\in\mathcal R}g_{\widehat r}.$ The test rests on the following assumption.

- **Gaussian assumption:** $g_{\widehat r}\overset{\mathrm{IID}}{\sim}N(0,\tau_g^2)$ for any annotator $r.$

Under this assumption, $g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}\sim N(0,\tau_g^2/K),$ so

$$
|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq z_{1-\alpha_g/2}\frac{\tau_g}{\sqrt K}
\quad\text{w.p. }1-\alpha_g.
$$ {#eq-gaussian-tail}

This is where the number of annotators enters.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Why the Gaussian assumption is plausible"}

The surrogate predictor of annotator $r$ differs from the latent target by $\widehat\mu_r-\mu^*=b_r+\widehat e_r,$ the bias of $r$ plus its learning error. Since B's annotation noise is centered, $g_{\widehat r}$ splits accordingly:

$$
g_{\widehat r}
=\mathbb E_X\big[b_r(X)(\widehat\mu_A(X)-\mu_B(X))\big]
+\mathbb E_X\big[\widehat e_r(X)(\widehat\mu_A(X)-\mu_B(X))\big].
$$

The second term vanishes for every $r$ by @eq-reference-orthogonality, so $g_{\widehat r}$ equals the first term. Conditional on $\widehat\mu_A$ and B, the first term is random only through which annotator is drawn. Suppose that for any finite collection of items $x_1,\ldots,x_n,$ the vector $(b_r(x_1),\ldots,b_r(x_n))$ is jointly Gaussian over the annotator population. Then the finite-sample version of the first term,

$$
\frac1n\sum_{i=1}^n b_r(x_i)(\widehat\mu_A(x_i)-\mu_B(x_i)),
$$

is a linear combination of a jointly Gaussian vector and is therefore Gaussian. As $n$ grows, with $x_1,\ldots,x_n$ drawn from the item distribution, this average converges to the first term of $g_{\widehat r},$ and a limit of Gaussian variables is Gaussian.
:::

#### Calibrating the scale without the latent target

The bound @eq-gaussian-tail depends on the unknown scale $\tau_g.$ Each $g_{\widehat r}$ involves the latent target, but the difference between two of them does not:

$$
g_{\widehat r}-g_{\widehat s}
=\mathbb E_{X,\epsilon}[(\widehat\mu_r(X)-\widehat\mu_s(X))(\widehat\mu_A(X)-Y_B(X))].
$$

These differences can therefore be estimated on $D_2$ by averaging $(\widehat\mu_r(X_i)-\widehat\mu_s(X_i))(\widehat\mu_A(X_i)-Y_B(X_i))$ over its images. Under the Gaussian assumption, the spread of these estimates across the reference annotators reflects $\tau_g,$ so inverting a chi-square test on them gives an upper confidence bound $U_g$ with $\Pr(\tau_g\leq U_g)\geq1-\gamma+o(1)$ as $n_2\to\infty.$ Substituting $U_g$ into @eq-gaussian-tail, we have

$$
|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq B_{\mathcal R}:=z_{1-\alpha_g/2}\frac{U_g}{\sqrt K}
\quad\text{w.p. at least }1-\alpha_g-\gamma+o(1).
$$ {#eq-gaussian-bound}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Computing the upper bound for the scale"}

Take one reference annotator, indexed by $1,$ as the baseline, and for $r=2,\ldots,K$ let

$$
W_{i,r}
=(\widehat\mu_r(X_i)-\widehat\mu_1(X_i))(\widehat\mu_A(X_i)-Y_B(X_i)),
\qquad i\in D_2,
$$

so that the mean $\bar W_r$ of $W_{i,r}$ over $D_2$ estimates $g_{\widehat r}-g_{\widehat 1}.$ Let $\bar W=(\bar W_2,\ldots,\bar W_K)^\top$ and let $\widehat\Omega$ be the sample covariance of $(W_{i,2},\ldots,W_{i,K})$ over $D_2.$ Under the Gaussian assumption, $\operatorname{Var}(g_{\widehat r}-g_{\widehat 1})=2\tau_g^2$ and $\operatorname{Cov}(g_{\widehat r}-g_{\widehat 1},g_{\widehat s}-g_{\widehat 1})=\tau_g^2$ for $r\neq s,$ because all differences share the baseline. For a candidate value $t$ of $\tau_g,$ the covariance of $\bar W$ is therefore estimated by

$$
\widehat V(t)=t^2\big(I_{K-1}+\mathbf1\mathbf1^\top\big)+\widehat\Omega/n_2,
\qquad
Q(t)=\bar W^\top\widehat V(t)^{-1}\bar W .
$$

With $K$ fixed and $n_2\to\infty,$ $Q(\tau_g)$ converges in distribution to $\chi^2_{K-1}$ by the multivariate central limit theorem and Slutsky's theorem. Since $Q(t)$ is non-increasing in $t,$ inverting it at the lower $\gamma$ quantile $q_{\gamma,K-1}$ of $\chi^2_{K-1}$ gives

$$
U_g=\sup\{t\geq0:Q(t)\geq q_{\gamma,K-1}\},
$$ {#eq-scale-calibration}

with $U_g=0$ when the set is empty, and $\Pr(\tau_g\leq U_g)\geq1-\gamma+o(1).$ On this event and the event in @eq-gaussian-tail, $|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq z_{1-\alpha_g/2}\tau_g/\sqrt K\leq B_{\mathcal R},$ and a union bound gives @eq-gaussian-bound.

:::

#### Establishing the test

On $D_1,$ the gap $\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ is estimated by the average $\widehat\Delta$ of the image-level differences

$$
d_i:=(\widehat\mu_A(X_i)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X_i))^2
-(Y_B(X_i)-\widehat\mu_{\mathcal R}(X_i))^2,
$$

with standard error $\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat\Delta)=s_d/\sqrt{n_1},$ where $s_d$ is the sample standard deviation of the image-level differences $d_i.$ Following @eq-population-certificate, the test *certifies* the evaluation reference $\widehat \mu_{\mathcal{R}}$ for this comparison when

$$
\boxed{\quad |\widehat\Delta|-t_{n_1-1,1-\alpha_\Delta/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat\Delta)>2B_{\mathcal R}.\quad}
$$ {#eq-general-certificate}

When the reference is certified, the sign of $\widehat\Delta$ tells whether the model or B performs better. A certificate is false if the reference is in fact not reliable, that is, if $\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}\Delta^*\leq0.$ The test controls the probability of a false certificate by

$$
\Pr\!\left\{
\text{certificate issued and }
\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}\Delta^*\leq0
\right\}
\leq\alpha_\Delta+\alpha_g+\gamma+o(1),
$$ {#eq-false-certificate}

where $\alpha_\Delta,$ $\alpha_g,$ and $\gamma$ are the failure probabilities of the three bounds the test relies on: the confidence bound for the gap, the Gaussian tail bound @eq-gaussian-tail, and the upper bound $U_g$ for $\tau_g.$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Proof of the error bound"}

Suppose the reference is not reliable, $\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}(\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}+2g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}})\leq0.$ Then $0$ lies between $\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}$ and $\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}+2g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}},$ so $|\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq2|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|.$ Consider the events

- $E_1=\{|\widehat\Delta-\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq t_{n_1-1,1-\alpha_\Delta/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat\Delta)\},$ with $\Pr(E_1)\geq1-\alpha_\Delta+o(1)$ by the central limit theorem for the paired differences $d_i;$ on $E_1,$ $|\widehat\Delta|-t_{n_1-1,1-\alpha_\Delta/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat\Delta)\leq|\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|;$
- $E_2=\{\tau_g\leq U_g\},$ with $\Pr(E_2)\geq1-\gamma+o(1)$ by the calibration;
- $E_3=\{|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq z_{1-\alpha_g/2}\,\tau_g/\sqrt K\},$ with $\Pr(E_3)=1-\alpha_g$ by @eq-gaussian-tail.

On $E_1\cap E_2\cap E_3,$

$$
|\widehat\Delta|-t_{n_1-1,1-\alpha_\Delta/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat\Delta)\leq|\Delta_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq2|g_{\widehat{\mathcal R}}|\leq2z_{1-\alpha_g/2}\frac{U_g}{\sqrt K}=2B_{\mathcal R},
$$

so no certificate is issued. A wrong certificate therefore requires the complement of $E_1\cap E_2\cap E_3,$ whose probability is at most $\alpha_\Delta+\gamma+\alpha_g+o(1)$ by the union bound.

:::

### Experiment

#### Experimental setting

We use six radiologists R11–R16^[In VinDr-CXR, radiologists R11–R16 labeled images with few positive findings, whereas R8–R10 labeled images with more positive findings. The test treats the annotators as IID draws from one population labeling the same image distribution, so we choose A, B, and the reference annotators only from R11–R16, whose surrogate predictors are learned from the same case mix.] from the VinDr-CXR dataset. We run the test on every configuration, that is, every choice of a training annotator A and a human B among them, together with $K=2, 3,$ or $4$ of the remaining four as the reference annotators. As in [I.1](#aggregate-score), we work with the aggregate score throughout this part: the model and the surrogate predictors are trained to predict each annotator's aggregate scores, and B's aggregate scores enter the comparison. The images labeled by R11–R16 are split into training, validation, and test images. The model and the surrogate predictors are trained on the training images; the gap $\widehat\Delta$ is estimated on B's test images ($D_1$), and the scale $\tau_g$ is calibrated on B's validation images ($D_2$).

By @eq-false-certificate, the sum $\alpha:=\alpha_\Delta+\alpha_g+\gamma$ bounds the probability of a false certificate; we call it the *total error budget*. We split it equally among the three bounds, setting $\alpha_\Delta=\alpha_g=\gamma=\alpha/3,$ and run the test at $\alpha=0.01,$ $0.05,$ $0.10,$ and $0.20.$

#### Result

For each $K$ and $\alpha,$ we call the fraction of configurations in which the test certifies the reference the *certification rate*. A certification means that the $K$ reference annotators of that configuration form a reliable reference for the model-human comparison between $\widehat \mu_A$ and $Y_B:$ their evaluation reference names the same better performer as the latent target, up to a false-certification probability of at most $\alpha.$ @fig-continuous-task2 shows that it increases with the total error budget and with the number of reference annotators. At $\alpha=0.20,$ the test certifies $10\%$ of the configurations with two reference annotators, $23.3\%$ with three, and $46.7\%$ with four. More reference annotators shrink $B_{\mathcal R},$ through the factor $1/\sqrt K$ and through a calibration of $\tau_g$ with more degrees of freedom, so smaller gaps between the model and B can be certified.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Experimental details"}

The $5{,}438$ images labeled by at least one of R11–R16 are split into $2{,}887$ training, $738$ validation, and $1{,}813$ test images. The $30$ ordered pairs (A, B) give $330$ configurations per total error budget: $180$ with $2$ reference annotators, $120$ with $3,$ and $30$ with $4.$ Each percentage is the number of certifications divided by the number of configurations in that cell; select a cell in the heatmap to see its count. Pooled over $K,$ the test certifies $2,$ $10,$ $21,$ and $60$ of the $330$ configurations at total error budgets $0.01,$ $0.05,$ $0.10,$ and $0.20.$

:::

#### Result for each configuration

The table below lists the decision of the test for each configuration. For a chosen pair of A and B and a chosen total error budget, each row is one set of reference annotators. The *observed gap* is $|\widehat\Delta|,$ the estimated gap between the model and B against the evaluation reference of these annotators. The *required gap* is $t_{n_1-1,1-\alpha_\Delta/2}\,\widehat{\mathrm{se}}(\widehat\Delta)+2B_{\mathcal R},$ the smallest observed gap that satisfies @eq-general-certificate. The reference is certified (✓) when the observed gap exceeds the required gap.

In the table, the menu *Comparison* selects the pair, written as "A-trained model vs B", and the buttons select the total error budget. Rows are grouped by the number of reference annotators $K,$ and certified rows are highlighted. Selecting a row shows below the table how its decision is reached.
